Aberts_Towhee.Description:
Brown overall with rusty crown and face. Pale throat contrasts with
dark spot on belly. Compact finch-like body, black tail. Subtle coloring
blends into desert brush easily.
Aberts_Towhee.Behavior:
Ground forager scratching in leaf litter and desert scrub. Moves with
quick hops and pauses. Often stays low in dense vegetation. Usually seen
singly or in pairs year-round.
Aberts_Towhee.Habitat:
Desert scrubland, mesquite thickets, and dry washes of southwestern
Arizona and New Mexico. Prefers thick brush near water sources. Resident
year-round in its range.
Aberts_Towhee.Similar Looking Birds:
Brown Towhee shares habitat but has brown crown and underparts. California
Towhee lacks rusty coloring. Green-tailed Towhee shows rufous crown and
greenish back in migrants.
Aberts_Towhee.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for rusty cap and face contrasting with brown body. Dark spot on
pale belly is distinctive. Scratching behavior on ground characteristic.
Listen for sharp call notes in desert brush areas.

Acadian_Flycatcher.Description:
Olive-green upperparts with yellowish underparts.
Pale yellowish eye-ring. Thin pointed bill adapted
for catching insects mid-flight. Small songbird
weighing only 9-12 grams.
Acadian_Flycatcher.Behavior:
Sits upright on perches watching for flying insects.
Sallies out quickly to snap insects from the air.
Territorial songbird with distinctive loud call.
Often returns to same perch after catching prey.
Acadian_Flycatcher.Habitat:
Deciduous and mixed forests with dense vegetation.
Favors areas near streams and swampy woodlands.
Breeds in eastern United States during spring
and summer migration season.
Acadian_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds:
Yellow-bellied Flycatcher has more yellow overall.
Least Flycatcher is grayer with different eye pattern.
Willow Flycatcher resembles Acadian but has
duller coloring and different call.
Acadian_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify:
Listen for loud distinct "pit-zup" call.
Note olive-green back with pale eye-ring.
Watch for active insect-catching behavior.
Observe thin pointed bill and upright posture.

Acorn_Woodpecker.Description: The Acorn Woodpecker is a striking woodpecker with a black and white face, bright red crown, and olive-green back. Males have a red crown extending to the nape, while females show a yellow-and-black patch. Both sexes display prominent white eye-rings, black chin, and white rump patches. Size: 8-9 inches long.
Acorn_Woodpecker.Behavior: Acorn Woodpeckers are highly social and live in cooperative family groups. They are known for drilling thousands of small holes in trees to store acorns, creating distinctive "granaries." They communicate with loud, raucous calls and engage in acrobatic foraging displays.
Acorn_Woodpecker.Habitat: Found primarily in oak woodlands and mixed forests from Oregon to Mexico. They prefer areas with large oak trees that provide acorns for food storage. Prefer elevations between 2,000-8,000 feet in diverse woodland ecosystems.
Acorn_Woodpecker.Similar Looking Birds: Can be confused with other woodpeckers like Pileated or Hairy Woodpeckers, but the distinctive red crown, white face pattern, and olive-green back are unique to Acorn Woodpeckers. Their social behavior and visible granaries help distinguish them.
Acorn_Woodpecker.Best Ways to Identify: Look for the striking white face with red crown, olive back, and white rump. Listen for loud, nasal calls. Search for distinctive granaries--trees covered with small holes. Their social behavior and noisy groups make them conspicuous in oak woodlands.

African_Collared-Dove.Description:
Medium pale dove. Very pale sandy-pink body with
thin black hindneck collar. White undertail coverts.
About 11 inches. Origin of domestic Ringneck Dove.
African_Collared-Dove.Behavior:
Forages for seeds and grain on ground. Ancestor of
domestic Ringneck Dove. Feral birds found in
Florida and other warm US areas.
African_Collared-Dove.Habitat:
Desert scrub and open areas in native Africa.
In North America found as feral birds in Florida,
occasionally elsewhere in the South.
African_Collared-Dove.Similar Looking Birds:
Eurasian Collared-Dove very similar but larger and
darker. African paler and more delicate.
African_Collared-Dove.Best Ways to Identify:
Very pale sandy-white plumage with thin black neck
collar. Smaller and paler than Eurasian
Collared-Dove. Found in Florida.

African_Silverbill.Description:
Tiny finch, pale sandy-brown above, white below,
pointed tail, pale silvery
bill. About 4 inches.
African_Silverbill.Behavior:
Highly gregarious in flocks. Nests colonially. Forages
for grass seeds. Introduced
to Hawaii and other areas.
African_Silverbill.Habitat:
Dry grasslands, scrub, and open areas. Introduced
to Hawaii and Florida.
Native to Africa.
African_Silverbill.Similar Looking Birds:
Indian Silverbill similar but darker brown. Munias
have heavier bills and
different tail shape.
African_Silverbill.Best Ways to Identify:
Pale sandy-brown with silvery bill and pointed tail.
Tiny size. Gregarious
in flocks. Hawaii introduced.

Agami_Heron.Description:
A stunning medium-large heron with deep chestnut and green plumage,
a bright blue and white neck, and a long, sharp dagger-like bill.
Agami_Heron.Behavior:
Stands motionless in shallow water or on riverbanks, then strikes
rapidly to catch fish. Solitary and secretive, rarely seen in open areas.
Agami_Heron.Habitat:
Dense tropical rainforest streams, swamps, and slow-moving rivers
from southern Mexico through Central America to South America.
Agami_Heron.Similar Looking Birds:
No other heron shares its vivid chestnut, green, and blue coloration.
Juvenile birds are brown and streaked, resembling immature night-herons.
Agami_Heron.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for the brilliant blue-white neck, chestnut body, and extremely
long bill. Its preference for shaded forest streams makes it distinctive.

Ainleys_Storm-Petrel.Description:
A small, all-dark sooty-brown storm-petrel with a slightly forked tail
and relatively short, rounded wings. Nearly identical to Leach's Storm-Petrel.
Ainleys_Storm-Petrel.Behavior:
Flies low over the ocean with erratic, bounding wingbeats. Breeds in
winter on rocky island cliffs, returning to colonies only at night.
Ainleys_Storm-Petrel.Habitat:
Open Pacific Ocean waters, breeding exclusively on Guadalupe Island
off Baja California, Mexico. Critically endangered with roughly 500 individuals.
Ainleys_Storm-Petrel.Similar Looking Birds:
Almost identical to Leach's Storm-Petrel and Townsend's Storm-Petrel.
Best separated by breeding season and subtle differences in wing shape.
Ainleys_Storm-Petrel.Best Ways to Identify:
Extremely difficult to identify at sea. Breeds in winter (unlike Leach's),
and shows a slightly less prominent white rump patch with dark central line.

Akekee.Description:
Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, yellow-green with black
mask, crossed bill tips. Blue-gray
bill. About 4.5 inches.
Akekee.Behavior:
Uses crossed bill tips to open flower buds for
nectar and insects. Critically
endangered on Kauai.
Akekee.Habitat:
Native forests of Kauai above 3,500 feet.
Very small population remaining.
Akekee.Similar Looking Birds:
Kauai Amakihi lacks black mask and crossed bill.
No other bird has
bill tips crossing in Hawaii.
Akekee.Best Ways to Identify:
Black mask, yellow-green body, crossed bill tips.
Only on Kauai native forest.
Critically endangered.

Akiapolaau.Description:
Small Hawaiian honeycreeper with unique bill: short
straight lower mandible for
hammering, long curved upper mandible.
Akiapolaau.Behavior:
Uses lower mandible to hammer wood, upper bill
to probe for insects. Critically
endangered on Big Island.
Akiapolaau.Habitat:
Native koa and ohia forests of the Big Island
above 4,000 feet. Very few
individuals remain.
Akiapolaau.Similar Looking Birds:
No other bird anywhere has this unique two-part
bill function. Distinctive in
any Hawaiian forest.
Akiapolaau.Best Ways to Identify:
Unique bill: short lower mandible plus long curved
upper. Yellow male. Big Island
koa forest. Critically endangered.

Akikiki.Description:
Small gray-and-white Hawaiian honeycreeper,
4.5 inches long. Pale gray back,
white underparts, pinkish bill.
Akikiki.Behavior:
Acrobatic bark creeper foraging for insects.
Tame, often in pairs. Critically
endangered -- fewer than 50 remain.
Akikiki.Habitat:
Found only on Kauaʻi above 3,500 feet
in native wet forests. Depends on
ʻōhiʻa and koa trees.
Akikiki.Similar Looking Birds:
Could confuse with bright yellow-green Anianiau
or Kauaʻi ʻAmakihi. Japanese White-eyes
have distinctive white eye-ring.
Akikiki.Best Ways to Identify:
Watch for creeping along bark.
Gray-and-white plumage, no bold markings.
High elevation and Kauaʻi location key.
Listen for soft high-pitched calls.

Akohekohe.Description:
Medium Hawaiian honeycreeper, dark with orange nape,
white-tipped feathers throughout,
white curly crest. About 7 inches.
Akohekohe.Behavior:
Feeds primarily on ohia nectar. Critically endangered.
Restricted to high-elevation
forests of east Maui.
Akohekohe.Habitat:
Native wet ohia forests of east Maui above 4,500
feet. One of most endangered
birds in United States.
Akohekohe.Similar Looking Birds:
No similar bird in range. White curly crest and
orange nape unique. Dark
plumage with white tips.
Akohekohe.Best Ways to Identify:
White curly crest and orange nape unique. Dark body
with white speckles. High
Maui forest. Critically endangered.

Alder_Flycatcher.Description:
Small olive-green flycatcher with whitish underparts, two white wing
bars, and a faint eye ring. Very similar to Willow Flycatcher.
Alder_Flycatcher.Behavior:
Perches upright on shrub branches, sallying out to catch insects.
Males sing a distinctive "fee-BEE-o" song from exposed perches.
Alder_Flycatcher.Habitat:
Wet thickets of alder and willow along streams, lake edges, and
bogs across northern North America; winters in South America.
Alder_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds:
Nearly identical to Willow Flycatcher. Also resembles other Empidonax
flycatchers. Voice is the only reliable field distinction.
Alder_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify:
Listen for the "fee-BEE-o" song. Habitat in wet alder/willow thickets
helps confirm. Eye ring slightly more pronounced than Willow Flycatcher.

Aleutian_Tern.Description:
Medium tern. Gray above, white below, black cap
with white forehead, black bill. Very similar
to Arctic Tern in shape. About 13 inches.
Aleutian_Tern.Behavior:
Dives for small fish. Breeds in Alaska. Migrates
to western Pacific; winters in Southeast Asia.
Migration route poorly known.
Aleutian_Tern.Habitat:
Coastal Alaska. Breeds on beaches and tundra near
coast. Migrates west across Pacific. Winters
in Southeast Asia.
Aleutian_Tern.Similar Looking Birds:
Arctic Tern very similar. Aleutian Tern has gray
body and black bill (not red).
Aleutian_Tern.Best Ways to Identify:
Gray body (not white like Arctic Tern). Black
bill. Breeds only in Alaska. Distinct
white forehead patch.

Allens_Hummingbird.Description:
Tiny hummingbird with iridescent green back, metallic red crown, and golden-green underparts.
Males have brilliant red gorget. Females duller with red throat speckles. Length: 3.3 inches.
Allens_Hummingbird.Behavior:
Highly aggressive and territorial. Males perform elaborate dive displays producing loud
chirping sounds with tail feathers. Rapid wing beats (40-50 per second) create humming sound.
Feeds on flower nectar.
Allens_Hummingbird.Habitat:
Chaparral, oak woodlands, gardens, and coastal scrub. Prefers areas with flowering plants.
Year-round resident in coastal California. Altitudinal migrant in inland regions.
Allens_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds:
Rufous Hummingbird (reddish overall), Calliope Hummingbird (smaller with purple gorget),
Costa's Hummingbird (purple crown and gorget). Ruby-throated Hummingbird (eastern range).
Allens_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for iridescent red-orange gorget on male. Bright metallic green back distinguishes from
Rufous. Listen for territorial dive display sounds. Females have red spots on throat. Fast,
direct flight pattern.

Altamira_Oriole.Description:
The largest North American oriole. Brilliant orange body with black
back, wings, and throat. Distinctive orange shoulder patch on wing.
Altamira_Oriole.Behavior:
Weaves a remarkably long hanging nest (up to 25 inches). Forages
in trees for insects, nectar, and fruit. Often seen in pairs.
Altamira_Oriole.Habitat:
Tropical woodlands, forest edges, and riparian areas from southern
Texas through Central America. Common in Rio Grande Valley.
Altamira_Oriole.Similar Looking Birds:
Resembles Hooded Oriole but is significantly larger and has an orange
shoulder patch. Audubon's Oriole has a black head, not throat patch.
Altamira_Oriole.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for the large orange shoulder patch and massive size. The black
throat combined with all-orange body is distinctive among Texas orioles.

Amaui.Description:
Medium Hawaiian thrush, brown-gray plumage. Known
only from Oahu. Extinct since
approximately 1825.
Amaui.Behavior:
Foraged for fruit in native Hawaiian forest.
Extinct before scientific study
could fully document its behavior.
Amaui.Habitat:
Native forests of Oahu, Hawaii. Extinct due
to deforestation and hunting
following Western contact.
Amaui.Similar Looking Birds:
Other Hawaiian Myadestes thrushes similar. All
extinct or endangered.
Amaui.Best Ways to Identify:
Extinct species from Oahu. No specimens with
complete description. Known from
subfossil remains and early accounts.

Amazon_Kingfisher.Description:
Large kingfisher with dark green upperparts and white underparts.
Male has a broad chestnut breast band; female has green-spotted flanks.
Amazon_Kingfisher.Behavior:
Perches over water, plunging headfirst to catch fish. Often solitary.
Gives a loud, rattling call. Territorial along riverbanks.
Amazon_Kingfisher.Habitat:
Rivers, streams, lakes, and lagoons in tropical lowlands from Mexico
through Central and South America. Prefers larger bodies of water.
Amazon_Kingfisher.Similar Looking Birds:
Similar to Green Kingfisher but much larger -- nearly twice the size.
Ringed Kingfisher is larger still and has rufous on both sexes.
Amazon_Kingfisher.Best Ways to Identify:
Large size distinguishes it from Green Kingfisher. Male's chestnut
breast band and female's spotted flanks are key field marks.

American_Avocet.Description: Elegant wading bird with distinctive upturned bill and striking plumage pattern. Black and white back and wings, white underparts, and rusty-chestnut head and neck during breeding season. Slender, long legs are blue-gray. Medium-sized and streamlined.
American_Avocet.Behavior: Highly social and gregarious, often seen in flocks both in breeding and non-breeding seasons. Feeds by sweeping its curved bill side-to-side through shallow water. Swift and agile flier, often flying in formation. Males perform elaborate courtship displays.
American_Avocet.Habitat: Prefers shallow alkaline lakes, salt marshes, and coastal lagoons. Breeds in loose colonies on sandy or rocky islands. Found in western North America, particularly in prairie regions and Great Basin. Migratory, wintering in southern coastal areas.
American_Avocet.Similar Looking Birds: American Avocet might be confused with other wading birds like stilts or whimbrels. However, its distinctive upturned bill and black-and-white pattern make it quite recognizable. Other avocet species occur in different geographic regions entirely.
American_Avocet.Best Ways to Identify: Look for the unique upturned bill, distinctive black-and-white plumage on back and wings, and long slender legs. The rusty head and neck appear in breeding plumage. Feeding behavior of sweeping bill side-to-side is very characteristic and distinctive among North American birds.

American_Barn_Owl.Description:
Distinctive heart-shaped white facial disc, tawny and gray mottled
upperparts, and pale white to buff underparts with fine dark spots.
American_Barn_Owl.Behavior:
Strictly nocturnal hunter that locates prey by sound alone in
total darkness. Gives eerie screeching calls instead of hooting.
American_Barn_Owl.Habitat:
Open grasslands, farmland, marshes, and woodland edges. Nests in
barns, tree cavities, and cliff ledges across North and South America.
American_Barn_Owl.Similar Looking Birds:
No other North American owl has the heart-shaped white face. Barn
Owls worldwide are similar but this species is unique in the Americas.
American_Barn_Owl.Best Ways to Identify:
Heart-shaped white face is unmistakable. Golden-buff back and white
underparts visible in flight. Active after dark near open farmland.

American_Bittern.Description:
Medium-sized heron with warm tan-brown and black streaking.
Yellowish-green legs, pale throat with dark stripe on neck.
Yellow-green facial skin around eye. Stocky build.
American_Bittern.Behavior:
Solitary, secretive bird that hunts in marshes from dawn to dusk.
Makes distinctive "thunder-pump" booming call in breeding season.
Freezes with neck extended vertically when threatened.
American_Bittern.Habitat:
Freshwater and brackish marshes with dense cattails and reeds.
Requires areas with standing water and tall emergent vegetation.
Prefers large reedbeds away from human disturbance.
American_Bittern.Similar Looking Birds:
Young Night-Heron has different body shape and neck pattern.
Least Bittern is much smaller and more delicate.
Immature herons lack the distinctive dark stripe on neck.
American_Bittern.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for cryptic brown streaking and stocky heron shape.
Listen for booming call in spring breeding season.
Watch for characteristic freezing posture with extended neck.

American_Black_Duck.Description:
A dark dabbling duck with predominantly blackish-brown plumage on head and body.
Males have bright reddish-purple bill and pale yellow feet. Females are similar but
slightly duller. In flight, pale underwings contrast sharply with dark body.
American_Black_Duck.Behavior:
Dabbling duck that feeds by tipping forward to reach submerged vegetation. Highly
social, often found in pairs or flocks. Dabbles in shallow water and grazes on land.
Males perform elaborate courtship displays. Relatively vocal with quacking calls.
American_Black_Duck.Habitat:
Inhabits freshwater marshes, swamps, ponds, and rivers in eastern North America.
Prefers shallow water with aquatic vegetation. Winters in coastal areas and open water.
Breeds in northeastern wetlands from Nova Scotia to Maine and adjacent regions.
American_Black_Duck.Similar Looking Birds:
Male Mallards have green head and white chest, unlike black duck's dark plumage. Female
Mallards show more contrast in pattern. Scoters are larger with different silhouette.
Pintails have elongated necks. Wigeon species lack dark coloring entirely.
American_Black_Duck.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for very dark overall plumage with pale underwings visible in flight. Males show
bright red-purple bill and yellow feet. White-spotted cheeks distinguish from Mallards.
Dabbling behavior at shallow edges. Pale eye-ring and head shape are also distinctive.

American_Coot.Description:
Medium-sized dark gray waterbird with black head and neck.
White bill and forehead shield. Distinctive red eye with
white inner ring. Compact body adapted for swimming.
American_Coot.Behavior:
Highly social and gregarious, often in large flocks.
Excellent swimmers but clumsy in flight. Makes loud
honking and cackling calls. Feeds by dabbling and diving
in shallow water and on land.
American_Coot.Habitat:
Found on freshwater lakes, ponds, marshes, and wetlands.
Prefers open water with emergent vegetation. Ranges from
southern Canada to Central America. Common in park ponds
and urban water bodies.
American_Coot.Similar Looking Birds:
Could be confused with Common Gallinule (red shield).
Gallinules have red bills and shields, Coots are white.
Juvenile Coots are lighter brown. Swimming waterfowl like
grebes have different body shapes and neck lengths.
American_Coot.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for distinctive white bill and frontal shield on
black head. Bright red eye is key field mark. Note white
under-tail coverts visible when swimming. Listen for
loud cackling calls year-round.

American_Crow.Description:
The American Crow is a large, all-black bird with a distinctive squared-off tail.
Its plumage is uniformly black with a slight iridescent sheen. Crows have a stout,
thick black bill and dark brown to black eyes. They measure about 16-21 inches long.
American_Crow.Behavior:
American Crows are highly intelligent and social birds, often found in flocks called
"murders." They are opportunistic foragers, eating insects, seeds, nuts, fruit, and
carrion. Known for problem-solving abilities and complex vocalizations beyond simple
caws. They can remember human faces and hold "grudges."
American_Crow.Habitat:
Crows thrive in diverse environments including forests, woodlands, farmland, parks,
and urban areas. They are highly adaptable and found throughout North America from
southern Canada to northern Mexico. They prefer open areas with nearby trees for
nesting and roosting.
American_Crow.Similar Looking Birds:
American Crows are often confused with ravens, which are larger with wedge-shaped tails.
Fish Crows are smaller and have a different call. Jays are colorful with crests. Grackles
are smaller with longer tails. Black Phoebes are much smaller. Starlings are smaller
with pointed bills.
American_Crow.Best Ways to Identify:
Listen for the distinctive loud "caw-caw-caw" call. Look for the squared-off tail
in flight, unlike ravens' wedge shape. Observe size compared to other birds--larger
than most songbirds. Watch for their habit of walking on ground. Crows often
gather in large flocks, especially at dusk.

American_Dipper.Description:
Small, stocky songbird with dark slate-gray plumage overall.
Distinctive rounded body shape with short tail and neck.
White eyelids flash when blinking. Bob their bodies constantly.
American_Dipper.Behavior:
Unique habit of walking underwater on stream bottoms to find food.
Dive and submerge in fast-moving water while hunting for insects.
Sing beautiful melodious songs, often near flowing water habitats.
Remain active year-round instead of migrating seasonally elsewhere.
American_Dipper.Habitat:
Fast-moving mountain streams and rivers with clear cool water.
Prefer rocky areas with waterfalls, cascades, and turbulent flow.
Found from sea level to high alpine elevations in western ranges.
Require streams with good water quality and adequate food sources.
American_Dipper.Similar Looking Birds:
Wrentit smaller with longer tail and different habitat preference.
Bushtit similarly small but found in dry chaparral, not streams.
Water-thrush breeds in eastern forests, different appearance.
Ouzel is another name for this species, not similar to anything.
American_Dipper.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for stocky dark bird bobbing while standing on rocks.
Watch for birds diving and walking on stream bottoms underwater.
Listen for loud melodious songs near fast-moving mountain water.
Note white eyelid flashes when bird blinks its eyes distinctly.

American_Flamingo.Description:
Brilliant pink plumage with long curved neck, stilt-like pink legs,
and a distinctive downward-bent black-tipped bill unique among birds.
American_Flamingo.Behavior:
Feeds by sweeping its inverted bill through shallow water, filtering
algae and crustaceans. Nests in dense colonies on mudflats.
American_Flamingo.Habitat:
Coastal lagoons, salt pans, and mudflats in the Caribbean and
extreme southern Florida. Requires warm, shallow alkaline waters.
American_Flamingo.Similar Looking Birds:
Roseate Spoonbill is also pink but has a flat spoon-shaped bill and
lacks the flamingo's long neck and distinctive kinked beak.
American_Flamingo.Best Ways to Identify:
Unmistakable brilliant pink color, extreme leg and neck length,
and unique bent bill visible at rest or while wading to feed.

American_Golden-Plover.Description:
Breeding adults have striking black face and underparts with
golden-speckled brown upperparts. Non-breeding birds are brownish
with pale eyebrow and golden spots on back.
American_Golden-Plover.Behavior:
One of the longest migrants in North America, flying from Arctic
tundra to South American grasslands. Runs along ground to forage.
American_Golden-Plover.Habitat:
Breeds on Arctic tundra. Migrates through prairies and coastal
mudflats. Winters on pampas grasslands in South America.
American_Golden-Plover.Similar Looking Birds:
Black-bellied Plover is larger with gray (not golden) upperpart
spots and shows white rump in flight. Pacific Golden-Plover is
nearly identical; best separated by call and primary projection.
American_Golden-Plover.Best Ways to Identify:
Golden-spotted back, slim build, small bill. Black belly and face
in breeding plumage is diagnostic. Look for primary tips extending
past tail tip at rest.

American_Goldfinch.Description:
Small finch with bright yellow plumage in breeding season. Males display vibrant
yellow with black wings and tail. Females and winter birds are duller olive-brown.
White wing bars and markings are distinctive year-round.
American_Goldfinch.Behavior:
Acrobatic fliers that often perform undulating flight patterns while calling.
Highly social, forming flocks especially in winter. They feed on seeds and
remain in groups while foraging and traveling.
American_Goldfinch.Habitat:
Open fields, meadows, and areas with thistle, dandelion, and weedy growth.
Orchards and gardens attract them when flowers and seeds are abundant. They
prefer semi-open areas with scattered trees and shrubs.
American_Goldfinch.Similar Looking Birds:
Female Orioles can be confused with female Goldfinches. Pine Siskins are
smaller and streakier. Lesser Goldfinches have white wing patches. Warblers
may appear similar in non-breeding plumage.
American_Goldfinch.Best Ways to Identify:
Listen for distinctive "per-chick-o-ree" call. Males in breeding season are
unmistakable bright yellow. Look for white wing bars on all birds. Undulating
flight with wings briefly closed is characteristic behavior.

American_Goshawk.Description:
Large powerful hawk with slate-gray upperparts, finely gray-barred
pale underparts, bold white eyebrow stripe, and vivid red-orange eyes.
American_Goshawk.Behavior:
Aggressive forest hunter pursuing birds and mammals at high speed
through dense trees. Fiercely defends nest, sometimes striking humans.
American_Goshawk.Habitat:
Breeds in mature boreal and montane conifer forests. Winters at lower
elevations; may irrupt into settled areas when prey populations crash.
American_Goshawk.Similar Looking Birds:
Cooper's Hawk is smaller with a rounded tail and less bold eyebrow.
Sharp-shinned Hawk is much smaller. Both lack the goshawk's size
and prominent white supercilium.
American_Goshawk.Best Ways to Identify:
Large accipiter size, bold white eyebrow, red eyes, and heavily
barred chest. Broad rounded wings and long tail visible in flight
through forest canopy.

American_Kestrel.Behavior:
Hovers above open fields hunting small prey. Hunts from perches and catches insects,
small lizards, and birds mid-flight. Often seen perched on telephone wires and posts.
Males perform dramatic diving displays during courtship season to attract females.
American_Kestrel.Habitat:
Open woodlands, grasslands, agricultural areas, and deserts. Favors open landscapes
with scattered perches. Found in meadows, prairies, and cultivated fields across
North and South America year-round or seasonally.
American_Kestrel.Similar Looking Birds:
Merlin is larger and lacks rufous coloring. Sharp-shinned Hawk is bulkier with longer
tail. Eurasian Kestrel males have solid gray heads. Female American Kestrels lack the
blue-gray wing pattern that males display prominently.
American_Kestrel.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for tiny falcon size with distinctive facial marks. Hovering flight is characteristic
of this species. Males show bright blue wing coverts in flight. Listen for rapid
"klee-klee-klee" call. Rufous back contrasts with blue-gray wings on males.

American_Oystercatcher.Description:
Large shorebird with striking black and white plumage. Head and upper body
are black, contrasting sharply with white belly and wing patches. Long,
straight, bright orange-red bill and legs. Eyes have golden-yellow iris.
American_Oystercatcher.Behavior:
Highly vocal and defensive of nesting territories. Forages along beaches
and mudflats probing or hammering at shells to extract mollusks. Often
seen in small flocks outside breeding season. Mates for life, often staying
with same partner for many years.
American_Oystercatcher.Habitat:
Found along coastal areas, beaches, sandy shores, and rocky coastlines.
Prefers salt marshes, tidal flats, and open beaches for feeding and nesting.
Ranges from Atlantic and Gulf coasts to Pacific waters throughout North and
South America.
American_Oystercatcher.Similar Looking Birds:
Black Oystercatcher (Pacific coast) differs in all-black plumage without
white belly. Other shorebirds like plovers and sandpipers are much smaller.
The distinctive orange bill sets them apart from almost all other species.
American_Oystercatcher.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for large black and white shorebird with unmistakable long orange-red
bill and orange legs. Listen for loud, sharp "kleep-kleep-kleep" calls.
Often seen in pairs or small groups probing beaches and mudflats for food.

American_Pipit.Description:
Small songbird with streaked, buffy-brown plumage and fine, pointed bill.
Pale underparts with streaking on breast and flanks. Darker back with
buff coloring. Slender build adapted for ground walking.
American_Pipit.Behavior:
Walks on ground with bobbing tail, rarely perches in trees. Often sings
from high perches during breeding season. Forages by walking and picking
insects from ground. Highly migratory, traveling between breeding and
wintering grounds.
American_Pipit.Habitat:
Breeds in alpine and arctic tundra above treeline. Prefers open, barren
terrain with sparse vegetation. Uses steep slopes, ridges, and rocky areas.
Winters in grasslands, desert scrub, and agricultural areas at lower elevations.
American_Pipit.Similar Looking Birds:
Resembles Sprague's Pipit but American Pipit has a slightly heavier bill
and different call. Red-throated Pipit in Asia. Lacks yellow in wings
unlike Meadow Pipit. Similar streaking pattern to some warbler species.
American_Pipit.Best Ways to Identify:
Listen for distinctive high-pitched calls and flight songs. Observe bobbing
tail motion when walking. Look for outer tail feathers with white spots.
Note thin, pointed bill. Watch for habit of walking on ground rather than
perching in vegetation. Breeding season males sing from exposed perches.

American_Pygmy_Kingfisher.Description:
Tiny kingfisher with dark metallic green upperparts, rich rufous-orange
breast and flanks, white belly, and a small dagger-shaped bill.
American_Pygmy_Kingfisher.Behavior:
Perches motionless on low branches over small forest streams and pools,
plunging headfirst to catch tiny fish, tadpoles, and aquatic insects.
American_Pygmy_Kingfisher.Habitat:
Dense tropical lowland forest streams, mangrove edges, and shaded
woodland pools from Mexico through Central and South America.
American_Pygmy_Kingfisher.Similar Looking Birds:
Green Kingfisher is noticeably larger with a heavier bill and more
white spotting. Amazon Kingfisher is much larger with a bigger crest.
American_Pygmy_Kingfisher.Best Ways to Identify:
Extremely small size is the best clue -- sparrow-sized. Rufous
breast contrasts with green back. Found over shaded, narrow forest
streams rather than open water.

American_Redstart.Description:
Small warbler with striking plumage. Males display black
head and back with bright orange-red patches on wings, tail,
and flanks. Females are gray with yellow-orange markings
instead of red, making identification challenging for beginners.
American_Redstart.Behavior:
Highly active flycatcher, constantly flitting and fanning tail
to flush insects. Males perform territorial songs from high perches
during breeding season. Females build cup-shaped nests in trees.
Often hover while catching prey mid-flight.
American_Redstart.Habitat:
Deciduous and mixed forests during breeding in North America.
Prefers young forest growth and forest edges with dense
understory. Winters in Central and South American tropical forests.
Found from Canada through Panama seasonally.
American_Redstart.Similar Looking Birds:
Female Redstarts resemble female Black-throated Blue Warblers
and Northern Parula. Young males can confuse with female plumage.
Bay-breasted Warbler shares some coloring. Key differences are
in head pattern and tail shape.
American_Redstart.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for orange-red tail patches and constant tail-fanning behavior.
Males unmistakable with black and red coloring. Females show orange-yellow
patches on wings and tail. Active feeding style in mid-canopy
distinguishes from perching warblers.

American_Robin.Description:
Medium-sized thrush with brick-red breast and upper abdomen. Gray-brown back,
white eye-ring, and distinctive white spots under tail. Males have darker head
and brighter coloring than females. Bill is yellow.
American_Robin.Behavior:
Hops along the ground searching for invertebrates. Often seen in a characteristic
upright posture. Loud, cheerful warbling song. Highly territorial during breeding
season. Forms flocks in migration and winter.
American_Robin.Habitat:
Found in open woodlands, parks, gardens, and urban areas. Breeds in forest edges
and clearings. Prefers areas with short grass for foraging and shrubs for nesting.
Highly adaptable to human-modified landscapes.
American_Robin.Similar Looking Birds:
Spotted Towhee has reddish flanks but black back and hood. Orchard Oriole females
are yellowish-green. Varied Thrush has orange wing bars and darker appearance in
western regions.
American_Robin.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for rusty-red breast and gray-brown back combination. Distinctive yellow bill
and eye-ring. Hopping behavior on ground is characteristic. Listen for loud, clear
warbling song. White spots under tail visible in flight.

American_Three-toed_Woodpecker.Description:
Medium woodpecker with black-and-white barred back,
yellow crown on male. Only three toes.
About 8 inches.
American_Three-toed_Woodpecker.Behavior:
Scales bark off dead trees to reach beetle larvae.
Boreal and mountain forest specialist.
More deliberate feeding than other woodpeckers.
American_Three-toed_Woodpecker.Habitat:
Boreal spruce-fir forest and high mountain conifers.
Often found in recently burned
forest areas.
American_Three-toed_Woodpecker.Similar Looking Birds:
Black-backed Woodpecker similar but has solid black
back. American Three-toed has barred back.
American_Three-toed_Woodpecker.Best Ways to Identify:
Barred black-and-white back. Yellow crown patch on male.
Three toes. Boreal and mountain
spruce-fir forest.

American_Tree_Sparrow.Description:
Small songbird with reddish-brown cap, gray face, and prominent black spot on
white breast. Grayish-brown upperparts and pale underparts. Fine bill adapted
for seed-eating. Similar size to House Sparrow but more delicate appearance.
American_Tree_Sparrow.Behavior:
Feeds on seeds and small insects, often in flocks during migration and winter.
Males sing from exposed perches in spring. Forages on ground or low vegetation.
Highly vocal with clear, tinkling song. Social and may visit feeders in winter.
American_Tree_Sparrow.Habitat:
Breeds in Arctic and subarctic regions of northern Canada, Alaska. Winters across
central and eastern United States in open fields, prairies, marshes, and weedy areas.
Prefers brushy terrain and shrubland with scattered trees near feeding areas.
American_Tree_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds:
Chipping Sparrow has similar size and coloring but lacks black breast spot. Field
Sparrow has pink bill and reddish face. Rufous-crowned Sparrow larger with different
head pattern. All smaller than Fox or Song Sparrows with more delicate features.
American_Tree_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify:
Black spot on white breast is the key field mark. Reddish crown combined with gray
face distinctive. Listen for clear, tinkling song in spring. Check for flocking
behavior in winter. Size and delicate appearance help distinguish from similar species.

American_White_Pelican.Description:
Large white waterbird with black wing tips, long bill, and large throat pouch.
Breeding birds display bright orange-yellow bill and facial skin patches. White
plumage contrasts with black flight feathers. Measures up to 5.5 feet in length
with a wingspan exceeding 9 feet, making them among North America's largest birds.
American_White_Pelican.Behavior:
Highly social birds, often found in flocks, hunting cooperatively by diving and
catching fish with their expansive throat pouch rather than spearing prey. They
are strong, graceful fliers that often soar on thermals at great heights. Pelicans
raft together on water and nest colonially in large groups on islands and sandbars.
American_White_Pelican.Habitat:
Inhabit shallow freshwater lakes, reservoirs, and coastal waters. Breed on
remote islands and sandy/rocky shorelines across western and central North America.
Winter primarily on southern U.S. coasts and Mexico. Prefer open water bodies with
adequate fish populations and minimal human disturbance for nesting colonies.
American_White_Pelican.Similar Looking Birds:
Brown Pelicans share similar body shape but are smaller, darker, and dive-fish
individually from flight. Trumpeter Swans are all-white but lack the prominent
throat pouch and have longer necks. Great White Herons are slimmer with thinner
bills. Wood Storks have curved bills and fly differently.
American_White_Pelican.Best Ways to Identify:
Massive size and white plumage with black wing tips are diagnostic in flight.
Distinctive large throat pouch, visible even at distance, is unmistakable. The
massive bill, much longer than any other North American waterbird, is a key field
mark. Watch for characteristic low, level flight pattern and cooperative feeding
behavior in large flocks on open water.

American_Wigeon.Description:
A medium-sized dabbling duck with males displaying a distinctive glossy
green head and white crown, with creamy-buff body and pale blue-gray
bill. Females are grayish-brown with mottled plumage and lack the
striking head pattern of males.
American_Wigeon.Behavior:
American Wigeons are highly social ducks, often seen in flocks grazing
on land and water. They feed by dabbling and upending, sometimes grazing
like geese. Known for their distinctive high-pitched whistle, males
produce a three-note "whee-whew-whew" call during breeding season.
American_Wigeon.Habitat:
Prefers shallow freshwater marshes, wetlands, and prairie lakes during
breeding season. Winters in coastal bays, estuaries, river valleys, and
agricultural areas. They inhabit both interior wetlands and coastal
regions throughout North America.
American_Wigeon.Similar Looking Birds:
Male American Wigeons can be confused with other dabbling ducks,
particularly Eurasian Wigeons which are rarer visitors. Females may
resemble female Mallards or Pintails but lack their distinctive patterns
and markings. Males are highly distinctive and unmistakable.
American_Wigeon.Best Ways to Identify:
Males are unmistakable with the white-crowned head and glossy green
face. Listen for the characteristic whistle. Females can be identified
by the dark eye, pale gray body, and smaller, more delicate build
compared to similar dabbling duck species.

American_Woodcock.Description:
Small, stocky shorebird with a long slender bill. Mottled brown and buff
plumage provides excellent camouflage in leaf litter. Eyes positioned high
on head for upward vision while feeding.
American_Woodcock.Behavior:
Crepuscular and nocturnal forager. Males perform spectacular spring displays
with twisting flights and nasal vocalizations. Probes soil for earthworms
and invertebrates with distinctive up-and-down head bobbing motion.
American_Woodcock.Habitat:
Prefers young forests, aspen thickets, and brushy areas with moist soil.
Found in eastern North America from Atlantic coast to Great Plains. Requires
both open areas for displaying and dense cover for nesting and resting.
American_Woodcock.Similar Looking Birds:
Wilson's Snipe has longer neck, different habitat preference. Both are
crepuscular shorebirds, but woodcock is more secretive. Common Snipe shows
more contrasting plumage patterns and prefers open wetland marshes.
American_Woodcock.Best Ways to Identify:
Listen for distinctive nasal "peent" call at dusk during spring. Look for
characteristic round, stocky body shape. Long bill and high eye placement
are diagnostic. Flight displays involve rapid twittering wing sounds.

Amethyst-throated_Mountain-gem.Description:
Medium hummingbird. Male green above with amethyst-
purple throat patch and white stripe behind eye.
Female green above, cinnamon below. About 4.5 inches.
Amethyst-throated_Mountain-gem.Behavior:
Feeds on nectar in mountain cloud forests. Rare vagrant
to Arizona from Mexico. Typically forages
at middle height in forest.
Amethyst-throated_Mountain-gem.Habitat:
Cloud forests and pine-oak mountain forests of Mexico.
Very rare vagrant to mountain
canyons of southeastern Arizona.
Amethyst-throated_Mountain-gem.Similar Looking Birds:
Blue-throated Mountain-gem similar habitat. Amethyst-
throated has purple throat and white supercilium.
Amethyst-throated_Mountain-gem.Best Ways to Identify:
Male's amethyst-purple throat patch and white stripe
behind eye. Green back. Very rare
vagrant in Arizona mountains.

Ancient_Murrelet.Description:
Small alcid. Black head and throat, gray back,
white underparts, white streaks on head in breeding.
About 10 inches.
Ancient_Murrelet.Behavior:
Nests in burrows on islands. Chicks leave at night
and swim to sea with parents. Migrates south in
winter. Winters off Pacific coast.
Ancient_Murrelet.Habitat:
Breeds on Pacific coast islands from Alaska south.
Winters offshore from Alaska to California.
Ancient_Murrelet.Similar Looking Birds:
Other small Pacific alcids. Black and gray pattern
distinctive.
Ancient_Murrelet.Best Ways to Identify:
Gray back with black head and throat. White head
streaks in breeding. Small alcid of
Pacific coast.

Anhinga.Description:
The Anhinga is a long-necked waterbird with dark, glossy plumage. Males are
black with silvery-white markings on wings and back. Females have brown necks
and breasts contrasting with darker bodies. Straight, pointed yellow bills and
serpentine necks are distinctive.
Anhinga.Behavior:
Anhingas dive deep underwater to hunt fish, using their sharp bills like
spears. They swim with bodies submerged, showing only their heads and necks
above water. They are excellent swimmers but rarely fly, spending most time
perched on branches drying their wings.
Anhinga.Habitat:
Found in freshwater lakes, swamps, marshes, and coastal waterways across
the southeastern United States through Central and South America. They prefer
shallow water with trees and vegetation for nesting and roosting. Common in
cypress swamps and mangrove areas.
Anhinga.Similar Looking Birds:
Cormorants share dark plumage and diving behavior, but have hooked bills and
thicker necks. Loons also dive for fish but are more compact. The Anhinga's
distinctive serpentine neck and straight spear-like bill set it apart from
these similar species.
Anhinga.Best Ways to Identify:
Look for the characteristic long, thin neck held in an S-curve. The pointed,
straight yellow bill is diagnostic. Watch for their habit of swimming low in
water with only neck and head visible. Silvery wing patterns visible in
flight help distinguish males from cormorants.

Anianiau.Description:
Tiny Hawaiian honeycreeper, bright yellow below, olive-yellow
above, short slightly
curved bill. About 4 inches.
Anianiau.Behavior:
Active nectar feeder in ohia and other flowers. One
of smallest Hawaiian honeycreepers.
Declining on Kauai.
Anianiau.Habitat:
Native wet and mesic forests of Kauai. Declining
but still present above
3,000 feet.
Anianiau.Similar Looking Birds:
Kauai Amakihi larger with longer curved bill. Anianiau
smallest yellow honeycreeper
on Kauai.
Anianiau.Best Ways to Identify:
Tiny bright yellow bird in Kauai native forest.
Short slightly curved bill.
Smallest honeycreeper on Kauai.

Annas_Hummingbird.Description:
Small hummingbird with iridescent rose-pink to magenta head and throat in males;
females and juveniles are green above with grayish-white below and spotted throat.
Annas_Hummingbird.Behavior:
Year-round resident; males perform dramatic diving courtship displays
producing loud popping sounds with tail feathers; aggressive defenders of feeders.
Annas_Hummingbird.Habitat:
Gardens, parks, open woodlands, and chaparral along the Pacific Coast
from Baja California to British Columbia; often near flowering plants.
Annas_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds:
Costa's Hummingbird has purple gorget extending to side tufts; Rufous Hummingbird
males are orange-rufous rather than deep rose-magenta.
Annas_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify:
Rose-magenta crown and gorget on males; larger size than most western hummingbirds;
metallic chirping song; present year-round on the West Coast.

Antillean_Nighthawk.Description:
Medium nighthawk with cryptically patterned brown,
black and buff plumage. White throat patch,
white wing bar in flight. About 9 inches.
Antillean_Nighthawk.Behavior:
Aerial insect catcher; forages at dusk and dawn.
Breeds in Florida Keys; winters in South America.
Call is distinctive "pilly-will-o-willy."
Antillean_Nighthawk.Habitat:
Open rocky areas, rooftops, and scrubby habitat
in Florida Keys and Caribbean islands. Winters
in northern South America.
Antillean_Nighthawk.Similar Looking Birds:
Common Nighthawk nearly identical. Antillean best
separated by call and range in Florida Keys.
Antillean_Nighthawk.Best Ways to Identify:
Best identified by distinctive "pilly-will-o-willy" call.
Nearly identical to Common Nighthawk visually.
Breeds in Florida Keys only.

Antillean_Palm_Swift.Description:
Tiny swift. Dark above with white rump, white
flanks and belly. Very small size and deeply
forked tail. About 4.5 inches.
Antillean_Palm_Swift.Behavior:
Nests in palm fronds in Caribbean. Fast twinkling
flight while foraging for aerial insects.
Rare vagrant to Florida from Caribbean.
Antillean_Palm_Swift.Habitat:
Found wherever palms grow in Caribbean islands,
especially Cuba, Hispaniola, and Jamaica. Rare
vagrant to southern Florida.
Antillean_Palm_Swift.Similar Looking Birds:
Other small swifts. White rump and flanks distinguish
Antillean Palm Swift.
Antillean_Palm_Swift.Best Ways to Identify:
Tiny size with white rump, white flanks, and dark
back. Deeply forked tail. Extremely rare
vagrant in southern Florida.

Apapane.Description:
Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, brilliant crimson-red
with black wings and tail,
white undertail. Curved bill. About 5.5 inches.
Apapane.Behavior:
Active nectar feeder in ohia trees. The most abundant
native Hawaiian bird. Chatters
and sings from treetops.
Apapane.Habitat:
Native ohia forests throughout Hawaiian Islands from
low to high elevations.
Most common native Hawaiian bird.
Apapane.Similar Looking Birds:
Iiwi larger with long curved salmon-pink bill.
Female not as brightly
colored but same pattern.
Apapane.Best Ways to Identify:
Brilliant crimson-red with black wings. White undertail.
Curved bill. Abundant in
ohia flowers throughout Hawaii.

Aplomado_Falcon.Description:
Elegant medium falcon, long tail, gray above with
distinctive facial pattern. Rufous belly
band, white below with dark flanks. About 15 inches.
Aplomado_Falcon.Behavior:
Reintroduced in southern Texas; hunts birds in open
grassland. Fast agile pursuit predator.
Aplomado_Falcon.Habitat:
Open grassland and coastal prairies. Reintroduced population
in southern Texas; also Mexico.
Aplomado_Falcon.Similar Looking Birds:
Peregrine Falcon heavier without rufous belly band.
Aplomado Falcon's distinctive face pattern.
Aplomado_Falcon.Best Ways to Identify:
Distinctive black-and-white face pattern with cream
supercilium. Rufous belly flanks. Elegant
long-tailed falcon.

Arctic_Loon.Description:
Medium loon, gray head in breeding, black and white
checkered back, distinctive white flank
patch. About 27 inches.
Arctic_Loon.Behavior:
Dives for fish in deep water. Breeds on Eurasian
and western Alaska tundra lakes.
Winters on Pacific coast.
Arctic_Loon.Habitat:
Tundra lakes in Eurasia and western Alaska. Winters
primarily on Pacific coast, especially
in Alaska waters.
Arctic_Loon.Similar Looking Birds:
Pacific Loon very similar. Arctic Loon has gray head
contrasting with black throat.
Arctic_Loon.Best Ways to Identify:
Gray crown and hindneck contrasting with black throat.
White flank patch visible on water.
Pacific coast in winter.

Arctic_Tern.Description:
Slender seabird with pale gray body, white cheeks, blood-red bill and legs,
black cap, and deeply forked tail; underparts whitish with translucent wingtips.
Arctic_Tern.Behavior:
Performs the longest migration of any animal -- from Arctic breeding grounds
to Antarctic wintering areas and back, traveling up to 70,000 miles yearly.
Arctic_Tern.Habitat:
Breeds on Arctic tundra and rocky coastlines; winters at sea near Antarctica;
found over open ocean during migration along both coasts and offshore.
Arctic_Tern.Similar Looking Birds:
Common Tern has orange-red bill with dark tip and less translucent wingtips;
Forster's Tern has frostier wing tips and is only found in North America.
Arctic_Tern.Best Ways to Identify:
All-red bill (no dark tip), translucent wingtip "windows" from below,
very long tail streamers, and buoyant graceful flight low over water.

Arctic_Warbler.Description:
Medium leaf warbler, olive-green above, whitish
below with single wing bar, long
supercilium. About 5 inches.
Arctic_Warbler.Behavior:
Breeds in willow scrub in Alaska; migrates across
Asia. Only Phylloscopus warbler
breeding in North America.
Arctic_Warbler.Habitat:
Willow and alder thickets in western and northern
Alaska. Winters in Southeast
Asia.
Arctic_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds:
Willow Warbler lacks wing bar. Yellow-browed Warbler
has two wing bars.
Kamchatka Warbler very similar.
Arctic_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify:
Single wing bar in Alaska breeding habitat. Long
supercilium, olive-green above.
Only breeder of its genus in Alaska.

Arizona_Woodpecker.Description:
Small woodpecker with solid brown back (unique among North American woodpeckers).
White underparts with dark spots. Males have red nape patch; females lack it.
Arizona_Woodpecker.Behavior:
Forages on bark of oak and pine trees searching for insects. Drums on dead
wood. Pairs stay together year-round in their territory.
Arizona_Woodpecker.Habitat:
Pine-oak woodlands in mountain canyons of southeastern Arizona and New Mexico.
Found at elevations of 4,000–7,000 feet. Closely associated with Arizona sycamore.
Arizona_Woodpecker.Similar Looking Birds:
Ladder-backed Woodpecker has barred black-and-white back. Hairy Woodpecker
has white back stripe. No other woodpecker has solid brown back.
Arizona_Woodpecker.Best Ways to Identify:
Solid brown back is diagnostic -- no other North American woodpecker has this.
Look in pine-oak canyons of southeastern Arizona. Listen for sharp 'peek' call.

Ash-throated_Flycatcher.Description:
Medium flycatcher with pale gray-white throat and breast, brownish-gray back,
rusty-red tail, and two faint whitish wing bars; belly faintly yellowish.
Ash-throated_Flycatcher.Behavior:
Catches insects by sallying from a perch; nests in tree cavities and nest boxes;
vocal with a variety of harsh "ka-brick" and rolling calls.
Ash-throated_Flycatcher.Habitat:
Dry open woodlands, desert scrub, and chaparral of the western United States
and Mexico; often near oaks or mesquite.
Ash-throated_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds:
Brown-crested Flycatcher is larger with stronger yellow belly; Great Crested
Flycatcher is brighter yellow below and found in the East.
Ash-throated_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify:
Pale ashy-white throat, rusty tail panels visible in flight, and dry open
western habitat; distinctive harsh "ka-brick" call.

Ashy_Storm-Petrel.Description:
Small, all-dark sooty brown seabird with forked tail. Pale gray wing linings
visible in flight. Slender build, fluttering wingbeats. About 8 inches long.
Ashy_Storm-Petrel.Behavior:
Feeds on small fish and crustaceans at sea surface, pattering feet on water.
Nests in rock crevices on offshore islands. Nocturnal at breeding colonies.
Ashy_Storm-Petrel.Habitat:
Pelagic waters of the California Current, mainly offshore California and Baja.
Breeds on Channel Islands and Farallon Islands. Rare vagrant elsewhere.
Ashy_Storm-Petrel.Similar Looking Birds:
Black Storm-Petrel is larger with slower wingbeats. Least Storm-Petrel is
smaller with wedge-shaped tail. Leach's Storm-Petrel has white rump.
Ashy_Storm-Petrel.Best Ways to Identify:
All-dark coloring, forked tail, and small size in California offshore waters.
Pale wing linings visible in good light. Rapid, fluttery flight pattern.

Asian_Brown_Flycatcher.Description:
Small flycatcher, gray-brown above, whitish below
with grayish-buff wash on sides.
About 5 inches.
Asian_Brown_Flycatcher.Behavior:
Sallies from exposed perch for flying insects.
Rare vagrant to western Alaska
and Aleutian Islands from Asia.
Asian_Brown_Flycatcher.Habitat:
Woodland and forest edges of Siberia and East
Asia. Rare vagrant to western
Alaska.
Asian_Brown_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds:
Gray-streaked Flycatcher has distinct breast streaking.
Dark-sided has darker sides.
Spotted Flycatcher streaked above.
Asian_Brown_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify:
Plain gray-brown above, pale below with buff wash
on sides. No streaking.
Very rare Alaska vagrant.

Asian_Rosy-Finch.Description:
Medium finch, brown with pink wing patches and
rump, gray crown. About 6 inches.
Asian_Rosy-Finch.Behavior:
Forages at snowfields and rocky alpine terrain for
seeds. Very rare vagrant to
western Alaska.
Asian_Rosy-Finch.Habitat:
Alpine and arctic terrain of Siberia and Asia. Very
rare vagrant to Alaska.
Asian_Rosy-Finch.Similar Looking Birds:
Black, Brown, and Gray-crowned Rosy-Finches all similar.
Pink wing patches shared
with all rosy-finches.
Asian_Rosy-Finch.Best Ways to Identify:
Brown body with pink wing patches and rump. Gray
crown. Very rare Alaska
vagrant from Siberia.

Atlantic_Puffin.Description:
Stocky seabird with striking black-and-white plumage; breeding birds have
colorful triangular bill banded orange, yellow, and blue-gray; orange feet.
Atlantic_Puffin.Behavior:
Dives underwater to catch small fish, carrying multiple fish crosswise in bill;
nests in burrows on rocky islands; silent at sea, grunting at colonies.
Atlantic_Puffin.Habitat:
Open North Atlantic Ocean when not breeding; nests on rocky islands and sea
cliffs from Maine and Maritime Canada to northern Europe and Iceland.
Atlantic_Puffin.Similar Looking Birds:
Razorbill has a thicker black bill; Common Murre is slimmer with no colorful
bill; Tufted Puffin has golden head tufts and is found in the Pacific.
Atlantic_Puffin.Best Ways to Identify:
Clown-like colorful triangular bill, round body, black back with white face,
and orange feet; seen flying low and fast over Atlantic waters.

Atlantic_Yellow-nosed_(Yellow-nosed)_Alb.Description:
Medium albatross, dark gray-black back and wings, white
body and head, black bill with yellow
ridge and red tip. About 32 inches.
Atlantic_Yellow-nosed_(Yellow-nosed)_Alb.Behavior:
Long-ranging pelagic seabird. Follows ships. Rare
vagrant to North Atlantic. Breeds on
South Atlantic islands.
Atlantic_Yellow-nosed_(Yellow-nosed)_Alb.Habitat:
South Atlantic Ocean. Rare vagrant to North Atlantic
coast; occasionally found off northeastern
North America.
Atlantic_Yellow-nosed_(Yellow-nosed)_Alb.Similar Looking Birds:
Black-browed Albatross similar but has yellow-orange
bill. Yellow-nosed has thin yellow bill ridge.
Atlantic_Yellow-nosed_(Yellow-nosed)_Alb.Best Ways to Identify:
Thin yellow ridge on black bill with red tip. White
head and underparts. Medium albatross
in the North Atlantic.

Audubons_Oriole.Description:
Large oriole, yellow-green body, black head, wings,
and tail. White wing bars.
About 9.5 inches.
Audubons_Oriole.Behavior:
Forages quietly in dense thorn scrub. Secretive for
an oriole. Resident in south
Texas brush country.
Audubons_Oriole.Habitat:
Dense thorn scrub and mesquite woodland of the
Rio Grande Valley and south
Texas.
Audubons_Oriole.Similar Looking Birds:
Scott's Oriole brighter yellow with different range.
No other yellow-green oriole
in Texas thorn scrub.
Audubons_Oriole.Best Ways to Identify:
Yellow-green body with all-black head and tail. Secretive
in dense Texas thorn
scrub. Resident species.

Audubons_Warbler.Description:
Yellow-rumped Warbler subspecies with yellow throat (not white). Males in
breeding plumage show yellow crown, rump, and sides. Gray back with streaks.
Audubons_Warbler.Behavior:
Active forager catching insects in flight and gleaning from foliage. Forms
large flocks in winter. Eats waxy myrtle berries when insects scarce.
Audubons_Warbler.Habitat:
Coniferous and mixed forests in western North America during breeding season.
Winters in open woodlands, shrublands, and coastal areas. Very adaptable.
Audubons_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds:
Myrtle Warbler (eastern Yellow-rumped) has white throat. Townsend's Warbler
has yellow face with dark cheek patch. Cape May Warbler has chestnut cheeks.
Audubons_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify:
Yellow throat combined with yellow rump is key. White wing patch visible in
flight. Western range separates from Myrtle Warbler. Chip call is sharp.

Aztec_Thrush.Description:
Medium thrush, dark brown above, white below with
bold brown spotting on breast,
white wing patches. About 9.5 inches.
Aztec_Thrush.Behavior:
Forages for fruit in pine-oak forests. Rare but
regular vagrant to Arizona and
Texas from Mexico.
Aztec_Thrush.Habitat:
Pine-oak forests of the Sierra Madre Occidental
in Mexico. Rare vagrant to
Arizona and west Texas.
Aztec_Thrush.Similar Looking Birds:
American Robin lacks bold white wing patches. Spotted
thrushes smaller and more
slender without wing patches.
Aztec_Thrush.Best Ways to Identify:
White wing patches obvious in flight. Spotted breast.
Dark brown above. Rare
Arizona vagrant from Mexico.

Azure_Gallinule.Description:
Small gallinule, pale blue with white underparts,
yellow bill, pink legs.
About 10 inches.
Azure_Gallinule.Behavior:
Walks on floating vegetation. Very rare vagrant to
eastern North America from
South America.
Azure_Gallinule.Habitat:
Floating marshes and grasslands of South America.
Very rare vagrant to eastern
North America.
Azure_Gallinule.Similar Looking Birds:
Purple Gallinule more colorful with red-and-yellow
bill. Common Moorhen darker.
Pale blue color distinctive.
Azure_Gallinule.Best Ways to Identify:
Pale blue with white underparts and yellow bill. Very
rare South American vagrant.
Small gallinule.

Bachmans_Sparrow.Description:
Medium sparrow, rusty-streaked above, plain buff
below, gray face, long rounded
tail. About 6 inches.
Bachmans_Sparrow.Behavior:
Sings beautiful, complex song from low perch. Extremely
secretive otherwise. Open
pine woodland specialist.
Bachmans_Sparrow.Habitat:
Open pine woodland with grass understory in southeastern
United States. Declining due
to habitat loss.
Bachmans_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds:
Botteri's Sparrow plainer above without rusty streaks.
Cassin's Sparrow in western
grasslands.
Bachmans_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify:
Rusty streaks on gray-brown back. Plain buff below.
Open pine woodland. Beautiful
clear whistled song.

Bachmans_Warbler.Description:
Small warbler. Male has black cap and bib, yellow
face and underparts, olive back.
Female greenish. About 4.5 inches.
Bachmans_Warbler.Habitat:
Bottomland swamp forests of southeastern United States.
Critically endangered or extinct.
Bachmans_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds:
Hooded Warbler has complete hood not partial. Wilson's
Warbler smaller. Yellow with
black cap and bib.
Bachmans_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify:
Possibly extinct. Male yellow with black cap and
bib. Bottomland swamp. Last
confirmed record early 1960s.

Bahama_Mockingbird.Description:
Large mockingbird, gray-brown above with streaked
sides, white underparts with streaking.
Two white wing bars. About 11 inches.
Bahama_Mockingbird.Behavior:
Bold and aggressive, defending territory vigorously.
Rare visitor to Florida Keys
and south Florida from Bahamas.
Bahama_Mockingbird.Habitat:
Thickets and scrub in the Bahamas. Rare visitor
to Florida Keys and extreme
southern Florida.
Bahama_Mockingbird.Similar Looking Birds:
Northern Mockingbird lacks streaking on sides and
has more white in wings.
Bahama_Mockingbird.Best Ways to Identify:
Streaked sides and flanks distinguish from plain
Northern Mockingbird. Florida Keys
vagrant. Larger overall.

Bahama_Swallow.Description:
Medium swallow with iridescent blue-green back, pure
white underparts, deeply forked tail.
About 6 inches.
Bahama_Swallow.Behavior:
Forages over open areas and pine forests. Rare
visitor to southern Florida.
Nests in tree cavities.
Bahama_Swallow.Habitat:
Pine forests of the Bahamas. Rare but regular
visitor to Florida Keys and
southern tip of Florida.
Bahama_Swallow.Similar Looking Birds:
Tree Swallow similar but less deeply forked tail
and different range. Cliff
Swallow has rusty rump.
Bahama_Swallow.Best Ways to Identify:
Pure white below, deeply forked tail. Iridescent
blue-green above. Florida Keys
visitor from Bahamas.

Bahama_Woodstar.Description:
Small hummingbird from Bahamas. Male has iridescent
rose-purple gorget, green back, white belly with
rufous flanks. Female greenish with spotted throat. About 3.5 inches.
Bahama_Woodstar.Behavior:
Feeds on nectar from various flowers. Found in
Bahamas; rare vagrant to Florida. Makes
seasonal movements among Bahamian islands.
Bahama_Woodstar.Habitat:
Scrub forest, gardens, and woodland in the Bahamas.
Rare visitor to southern Florida, particularly
the Florida Keys.
Bahama_Woodstar.Similar Looking Birds:
Ruby-throated Hummingbird similar size. Male Bahama
Woodstar's rose gorget and rufous flanks distinctive.
Bahama_Woodstar.Best Ways to Identify:
Male's rose-purple gorget and rufous sides distinctive.
Female's spotted throat. Very rare
vagrant in southern Florida.

Baikal_Teal.Description:
Small dabbling duck. Male has intricate mosaic head
pattern: green, buff, black and white panels. Female
brown with white spot near bill base. About 16 inches.
Baikal_Teal.Behavior:
Dabbles for seeds and aquatic plants in shallow water.
Forms massive flocks in East Asia during migration.
Rare vagrant to western Alaska from Siberia.
Baikal_Teal.Habitat:
Breeds in Siberian taiga wetlands and tundra marshes.
Winters in East Asian lakes, wetlands, and
flooded rice paddies.
Baikal_Teal.Similar Looking Birds:
Garganey similar size and shape. Female could
be confused with other female dabbling ducks.
Baikal_Teal.Best Ways to Identify:
Male's complex multi-colored head pattern unique in
North America. Female's white facial spot
at bill base and dark eye line distinctive.

Bairds_Sandpiper.Description:
Medium-small sandpiper with buffy-brown upperparts, scaly back pattern, and
whitish underparts with light breast streaking. Long wingtips extend past tail.
Slender, horizontal posture. About 7.5 inches long.
Bairds_Sandpiper.Behavior:
Forages on dry upland areas and mudflats picking invertebrates. Long-distance
migrant traveling from Arctic to South America. Often in small flocks inland.
Bairds_Sandpiper.Habitat:
Arctic tundra breeder. Migrates through Great Plains and mountain meadows.
Prefers dry, short-grass areas near water. Winters on South American grasslands.
Bairds_Sandpiper.Similar Looking Birds:
White-rumped Sandpiper also has long wingtips but has white rump. Pectoral
Sandpiper is larger with sharp breast band. Least Sandpiper has yellow legs.
Bairds_Sandpiper.Best Ways to Identify:
Long wingtips projecting well past tail tip -- key feature. Buffy-brown scaly
back. Slender horizontal posture. Dark legs. Migrates through interior plains.

Bairds_Sparrow.Description:
Medium sparrow, ochre-orange head with narrow streaks,
necklace of streaks on breast,
flat head. About 5.5 inches.
Bairds_Sparrow.Behavior:
Extremely secretive in grass, rarely flushing. Walks
on ground under dense grass.
Declining rapidly.
Bairds_Sparrow.Habitat:
Native mixed-grass and short-grass prairie of northern
Great Plains. Declining due
to grassland loss.
Bairds_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds:
Savannah Sparrow has bolder supercilium. Henslow's
Sparrow olive-green head.
Orange head with necklace streaks.
Bairds_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify:
Ochre-orange head with fine dark streaks. Necklace
of breast streaks. Northern
Great Plains grassland specialist.

Bald_Eagle.Description:
Large raptor with distinctive white head and tail contrasting with dark brown
body; bright yellow hooked bill and talons; wingspan up to 8 feet.
Bald_Eagle.Behavior:
Soars on flat wings; plucks fish from water with talons; steals food from other
birds (kleptoparasitism); builds massive stick nests reused for many years.
Bald_Eagle.Habitat:
Near large bodies of open water with abundant fish -- coasts, rivers, lakes,
and reservoirs; nests in tall trees or on cliffs near water.
Bald_Eagle.Similar Looking Birds:
Immature Bald Eagles are mottled brown; Osprey is smaller with crooked wings
and a dark eye stripe; Golden Eagle has golden nape and darker tail base.
Bald_Eagle.Best Ways to Identify:
White head and tail on brown body (adults); flat-winged soar; massive size;
yellow bill; found near water throughout North America.

Baltimore_Oriole.Description:
Striking male is brilliant orange with black hood, back, wings, and tail;
white wing bars. Female is olive-yellow with two white wing bars.
Baltimore_Oriole.Behavior:
Weaves a hanging pouch nest high in deciduous trees; eats insects, nectar,
and fruit; visits orange halves and grape jelly at feeders.
Baltimore_Oriole.Habitat:
Open deciduous woodlands, forest edges, parks, and suburban areas of eastern
North America; winters in Central America and northern South America.
Baltimore_Oriole.Similar Looking Birds:
Orchard Oriole male is chestnut and black, not orange; Bullock's Oriole male
has large white wing patch and orange face; Hooded Oriole is slimmer.
Baltimore_Oriole.Best Ways to Identify:
Brilliant orange and black male; hanging woven nest; rich whistled song;
common along forest edges and suburbs in summer in the East.

Bananaquit.Description:
Tiny bird, black above with bold white supercilium,
bright yellow below, white wing
patch. About 4.5 inches.
Bananaquit.Behavior:
Pierces flower bases with sharp bill for nectar.
Very active and bold. Common
Caribbean species.
Bananaquit.Habitat:
Forest edges, gardens, and flowering trees. Established
in southern Florida. Common
throughout Caribbean.
Bananaquit.Similar Looking Birds:
No similar bird with black above and yellow below
plus bold white supercilium.
Distinctive pattern.
Bananaquit.Best Ways to Identify:
Black above with bold white supercilium and bright
yellow below. Tiny size.
Florida and Caribbean.

Band-rumped_Storm-Petrel.Description:
Medium storm-petrel with dark brown plumage and distinctive white rump band.
Square-tipped tail, long wings. Larger and heavier-looking than Leach's.
About 9 inches long with buoyant, shearwater-like flight.
Band-rumped_Storm-Petrel.Behavior:
Feeds on small fish and squid by surface-pattering or dipping. Nests in
burrows on oceanic islands. Has two separate breeding cycles per island.
Band-rumped_Storm-Petrel.Habitat:
Tropical and subtropical Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Rare but regular off
U.S. Atlantic coast, especially after storms. Breeds on Galapagos and Hawaii.
Band-rumped_Storm-Petrel.Similar Looking Birds:
Leach's Storm-Petrel has forked tail and erratic flight. Wilson's Storm-Petrel
has yellow-webbed feet visible in flight. Ashy is smaller and darker overall.
Band-rumped_Storm-Petrel.Best Ways to Identify:
White rump band with square tail (not forked like Leach's). Shearwater-like
gliding flight. Larger size than most storm-petrels. Atlantic offshore records.

Band-tailed_Pigeon.Description:
Large pigeon with gray body, purplish head and breast, yellow bill with dark
tip, yellow feet, and distinctive white crescent on nape; gray tail band.
Band-tailed_Pigeon.Behavior:
Flocks heavily in fall to feed on acorns and berries; migrates in large flocks;
makes deep cooing calls; nests in Douglas fir and other conifers.
Band-tailed_Pigeon.Habitat:
Mountain forests of the Pacific Coast and Southwest; found in oak and mixed
conifer forests; sometimes descends to lowland orchards in winter.
Band-tailed_Pigeon.Similar Looking Birds:
Rock Pigeon (city pigeon) has iridescent neck and lacks white nape crescent;
Mourning Dove is slimmer with pointed tail and spotted wings.
Band-tailed_Pigeon.Best Ways to Identify:
Large gray pigeon with white crescent on nape, yellow bill tip, and yellow
feet; flocks in mountain oak and conifer forests of the West.

Bank_Swallow.Description:
Small swallow, brown above, white below with brown
chest band. Small bill.
About 5 inches.
Bank_Swallow.Behavior:
Nests colonially in burrows in riverbanks and sand
cliffs. Forages over water for
flying insects.
Bank_Swallow.Habitat:
Riverbanks with sandy bluffs for nesting; forages
over water bodies across North
America. Migratory.
Bank_Swallow.Similar Looking Birds:
Rough-winged Swallow lacks chest band, has brown
throat. Tree Swallow has
iridescent blue-green back.
Bank_Swallow.Best Ways to Identify:
Brown chest band across white underparts. Brown
back. Colonial nester in
sand bank burrows.

Bar-tailed_Godwit.Description:
Large godwit. Breeding male has reddish-orange underparts,
brown streaked back. Long slightly upturned bill.
Barred tail. About 16 inches.
Bar-tailed_Godwit.Behavior:
Makes longest known non-stop migration of any bird:
Alaska to New Zealand (11,000 km non-stop). Forages
on mudflats for invertebrates.
Bar-tailed_Godwit.Habitat:
Breeds on Arctic tundra. Migrates through Pacific.
Winters on coasts of Australia and New Zealand.
Uncommon along Pacific coast.
Bar-tailed_Godwit.Similar Looking Birds:
Hudsonian Godwit has white wing stripe. Bar-tailed
has barred tail and streaked back.
Bar-tailed_Godwit.Best Ways to Identify:
Barred tail and streaked (not white) back. No
white wing stripe visible in flight.
Longest non-stop migration of any bird.

Bare-throated_Tiger-Heron.Description:
Large heron with finely barred brown and black plumage
("tiger" pattern), bare orange-yellow
throat. About 32 inches.
Bare-throated_Tiger-Heron.Behavior:
Stalks fish in tropical waterways. Stands motionless
then strikes. Very rare vagrant
from Mexico to southern Texas.
Bare-throated_Tiger-Heron.Habitat:
Tropical rivers and mangroves from Mexico to South
America. Very rare vagrant to
southern Texas.
Bare-throated_Tiger-Heron.Similar Looking Birds:
No other North American heron has tiger-barred plumage
with bare yellow throat.
Bare-throated_Tiger-Heron.Best Ways to Identify:
Finely barred black-and-brown plumage distinctive.
Bare orange-yellow throat. Very rare
Texas vagrant from Mexico.

Barn_Owl.Description:
Ghost-pale owl with distinctive heart-shaped white facial disc; golden-buff
above with gray and fine dark markings; white to pale buff below.
Barn_Owl.Behavior:
Nocturnal; hunts by sound alone in total darkness; swallows prey whole and
regurgitates compact pellets; screams rather than hoots; nests in barns and cavities.
Barn_Owl.Habitat:
Open country -- farmland, grasslands, marshes, and lightly wooded areas; one
of the world's most widely distributed birds, found on every continent except Antarctica.
Barn_Owl.Similar Looking Birds:
Barred Owl has streaked brown plumage and dark eyes; Snowy Owl is much
larger and all-white; Short-eared Owl has yellow eyes and streaked plumage.
Barn_Owl.Best Ways to Identify:
Heart-shaped white face disc, ghostly pale plumage, and silent moth-like
flight; screaming call; associates with open farmland and old buildings.

Barn_Swallow.Description:
Sleek swallow with deep blue-black back, rusty-orange throat and forehead,
pale buff belly, and long deeply forked tail streamers (longer in males).
Barn_Swallow.Behavior:
Catches insects in graceful aerial pursuit; nests in open buildings, bridges,
and culverts using mud pellets; the world's most widespread swallow species.
Barn_Swallow.Habitat:
Open country near water -- farmland, meadows, marshes, and ponds; found
throughout North America in summer; winters in South America.
Barn_Swallow.Similar Looking Birds:
Cliff Swallow has square tail and white forehead; Purple Martin is much larger
and all-dark; Tree Swallow has white belly and green-blue back.
Barn_Swallow.Best Ways to Identify:
Deep forked tail, rusty-orange throat, blue-black back; graceful swooping
flight over fields and water; nests in barns and under bridges.

Barnacle_Goose.Description:
Medium goose with white face and forehead contrasting with black crown, neck,
and breast. Gray barred back. White belly. Short black bill. About 27 inches.
Barnacle_Goose.Behavior:
Grazes on grasses and agricultural fields. Highly social, forming large flocks.
Nests on cliff ledges in the Arctic to avoid predators. Strong migratory flier.
Barnacle_Goose.Habitat:
Arctic tundra for breeding; coastal grasslands and estuaries in winter. Rare
visitor to northeastern North America, mainly Atlantic coast. Eurasian species.
Barnacle_Goose.Similar Looking Birds:
Canada Goose has brown body and lacks white face. Cackling Goose is similar
but has no white face. Brant has dark belly and no white face pattern.
Barnacle_Goose.Best Ways to Identify:
White face and forehead on black head is unmistakable. Gray barred back, black
breast. In North America, check eastern coastal areas for rare vagrant records.

Barolo_Shearwater.Description:
Tiny shearwater, black above, white below with white
wrapping around rear of face and neck.
Black bill and feet. About 10 inches.
Barolo_Shearwater.Behavior:
Breeds on Macaronesian islands (Azores, Canaries).
Rare vagrant to North American Atlantic
coast.
Barolo_Shearwater.Habitat:
Eastern North Atlantic. Rare vagrant to North American
Atlantic coast, particularly
off North Carolina.
Barolo_Shearwater.Similar Looking Birds:
Manx Shearwater larger. Barolo very tiny, white wrapping
around rear of face.
Barolo_Shearwater.Best Ways to Identify:
Tiny size, black above with white below wrapping around
face sides. Rare Atlantic vagrant.
Smallest Atlantic shearwater.

Barred_Owl.Description:
Large, stocky, round-headed owl with brown-and-white barred upper chest
and brown-streaked white belly; dark eyes; no ear tufts; brown-gray overall.
Barred_Owl.Behavior:
Nocturnal hunter of small mammals, frogs, and birds; famous "who cooks for
you, who cooks for you-all" hooting call; expanding range westward.
Barred_Owl.Habitat:
Dense mature forests, swamps, and river bottomlands of eastern North America
and now Pacific Northwest; roosts in dense foliage during the day.
Barred_Owl.Similar Looking Birds:
Spotted Owl (closely related) has spots rather than streaks on belly; Great
Horned Owl has ear tufts and yellow eyes; Barn Owl has heart-shaped face.
Barred_Owl.Best Ways to Identify:
Horizontal barring on chest, vertical brown streaking on belly, dark eyes,
and distinctive loud "who cooks for you" hooting call.

Barrows_Goldeneye.Description:
Medium diving duck. Male has black and white
plumage, purplish-green iridescent head with white
crescent spot near bill. Female gray-brown. About 18 inches.
Barrows_Goldeneye.Behavior:
Dives for aquatic invertebrates and fish. Nests
in tree cavities near lakes. Less common
than Common Goldeneye in most areas.
Barrows_Goldeneye.Habitat:
Breeds on montane lakes in western North America
and Iceland. Winters along Pacific coast and
inland western lakes and rivers.
Barrows_Goldeneye.Similar Looking Birds:
Common Goldeneye nearly identical. Male has circular
head spot and greenish head gloss.
Barrows_Goldeneye.Best Ways to Identify:
Male's crescent-shaped face spot versus round spot
in Common Goldeneye. Steeper forehead
profile. Female's mostly yellow bill.

Bat_Falcon.Description:
Small falcon, black above, white throat and chest,
rufous belly and thighs. White spots
on crown. About 10 inches.
Bat_Falcon.Behavior:
Hunts bats and small birds at dawn and dusk. Very
rare vagrant from Mexico to
southern Texas.
Bat_Falcon.Habitat:
Forest edges and clearings of Mexico and Central
America. Very rare vagrant to
southern Texas.
Bat_Falcon.Similar Looking Birds:
American Kestrel different plumage. Bat Falcon's black-
and-rufous pattern distinctive.
Bat_Falcon.Best Ways to Identify:
Black above, rufous belly, white throat. Very small
falcon. Crepuscular habits. Rare
vagrant from Mexico.

Bay-breasted_Warbler.Description:
Breeding male has chestnut (bay) crown, throat, and sides; black face; cream
neck patch; white wing bars. Female and fall birds are much duller.
Bay-breasted_Warbler.Behavior:
Forages methodically through dense conifer foliage for caterpillars; a spruce
budworm specialist whose populations fluctuate with budworm outbreaks.
Bay-breasted_Warbler.Habitat:
Boreal spruce-fir forests in summer; migrates through eastern North America;
winters in Panama and northern South America in forest canopy.
Bay-breasted_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds:
Chestnut-sided Warbler has yellow cap and white face; fall Bay-breasted is
very similar to fall Blackpoll Warbler -- look for buffy flanks.
Bay-breasted_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify:
Breeding male's deep chestnut crown and sides are diagnostic; fall birds show
buffy flanks and faint streaking; creeping foraging style in spruce tops.

Belchers_Gull.Description:
Medium gull. Black back and wings, white head and
underparts, yellow bill with black and red bands,
yellow legs. About 20 inches.
Belchers_Gull.Behavior:
Forages along Pacific coast of South America. Rare
vagrant to Pacific coast of North America from
Peru and Chile.
Belchers_Gull.Habitat:
Pacific coast of Peru and Chile. Rare vagrant to
California and Pacific coast.
Belchers_Gull.Similar Looking Birds:
Kelp Gull similar pattern. Belcher's has yellow
(not greenish) legs and different bill bands.
Belchers_Gull.Best Ways to Identify:
Black back, white head, and distinctive banded yellow
bill. Yellow legs. Rare vagrant
from South American Pacific coast.

Bells_Sparrow.Description:
Medium sparrow, gray-brown above, white below with
dark malar stripe, central breast
spot, dark lores. About 6 inches.
Bells_Sparrow.Behavior:
Runs on ground under dense scrub rather than flying.
Forages for seeds and insects.
Secretive.
Bells_Sparrow.Habitat:
Coastal sage scrub, saltbush, and dense chaparral
of California and northern
Baja California.
Bells_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds:
Sagebrush Sparrow very similar but in different habitat.
Black-throated Sparrow has
black throat.
Bells_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify:
Dark malar stripe, central breast spot. Dense coastal
sage scrub California. Runs
on ground rather than flying.

Bells_Vireo.Description:
Small vireo, grayish above with two wing bars and
pale eye ring. Yellowish sides and
flanks. About 5 inches.
Bells_Vireo.Behavior:
Skulks in dense scrub. Song a fast rambling chatter.
Declining due to Brown-headed Cowbird
parasitism.
Bells_Vireo.Habitat:
Dense willow and mesquite scrub along streams. Breeding
range from Great Plains to
California.
Bells_Vireo.Similar Looking Birds:
